Man who used police ruse to assault girls jailed

The new centre adds 60,000sq ft (5,574sq m) of space to Vertical's existing flight test centre at Cotswold Airport.

Vertical said construction of the new aircraft would begin in late 2027 with an initial 25 being built every year before the company increases that number to 900 a year by 2035.

The company said it had 1,500 orders, many of which were from airlines.

It said there were plans to get the planes certified for commercial use by 2029.

Stuart Simpson said that we've moving closer to the idea of flying cars and flying taxis.

"Bringing a new category of aircraft to market is a once-in-a-generation opportunity and it is especially rewarding to do that here in Great Britain, drawing on the country's proud aviation heritage," he added.

McDougall said the assembly centre was "exactly the kind of investment we want to see more of as we work to reindustrialise Britain, creating high-skilled local jobs and strengthening our manufacturing base".

Suzannah Harvey, CEO of Cotswold Airport, said she was "delighted" to support the new centre which she said strengthened the airport's "growing role as a hub for aerospace innovation".

Plans for a separate full-scale production site, intended to support higher-volume manufacturing, are expected to be announced later this year.

articles.title: Lean Into the Wind on Bournemouth's West Cliff set to be finished
articles.summary: Lean Into the Wind is part of BCP Council's government-funded Coastal Public Art and Heritage Trail.
articles.body:
A new art sculpture is being installed on Bournemouth's West Cliff.

Lean Into the Wind is part of BCP Council's government-funded Coastal Public Art and Heritage Trail and reflects the town's coastline and identity.

It was developed with input from schoolchildren and community groups and the trail aims to encourage visitors to explore the area's heritage.

Andy Martin, BCP Council's cabinet member for culture, communications and customer, said: "Installation is now complete and the remaining temporary fencing will begin to be removed next week, with some low-level fencing staying in place for a short time to allow newly seeded meadow grass to establish."

He added: "The project cost £54,000 and was fully funded through a UK Government grant, meaning there was no cost to local taxpayers."

articles.title: V&A museum workers in London to strike over pay and conditions
articles.summary: A limited number of galleries will be open on Friday and Saturday at the museum's South Kensington site.
articles.body:
Museum workers at the V&A in London are to stage a two-day strike in a dispute over pay and conditions.

Members of Prospect and the Public and Commercial Services union (PCS) will walk out on Friday and Saturday, meaning only a limited number of galleries will be open.

Prospect is calling for a minimum 4% pay increase for staff earning above the living wage and other benefits including time-and-a-half for bank holiday working.

The strike action will only cover the museum's site in South Kensington but Prospect said it remained in dispute at other V&A sites across the capital.

Mike Clancy, general secretary of Prospect, said members had been left with "no choice" but to take action as senior management "continues to not engage seriously on our very reasonable demands".

He added: "Directors at V&A continue to demonstrate their lack of respect for the very people who make the museum what it is – its dedicated, highly qualified staff.

"The V&A can still avoid this strike, but it needs actual effort to meet our terms and for senior management to demonstrate that they are serious about wanting to find a solution."

The V&A said in a statement: "Due to planned industrial action on 25 and 26 September 2026, V&A South Kensington will be operating a reduced visitor offer.

"Schiaparelli: Fashion Becomes Art, the cafe and a limited number of galleries will be open, but we expect the rest of the museum will be closed."

Young V&A, V&A East Museum and Storehouse will be open as usual.

articles.title: An Italian town is rebuilding its school with 70% of the old building's demolition waste; it will also collect rainwater
articles.summary: An Italian town is replacing its existing primary school with a building designed to reuse the old structure’s demolition waste.
articles.body: An Italian town is replacing its existing primary school with a building designed to reuse the old structure’s demolition waste. The project in Castel Madama, called ‘New School: Innovation, Inclusion’, will reuse, recycle, or recover about 70% of the demolition waste from the existing school. According to the New European Bauhaus Prizes, it will collect rainwater and groundwater as part of the design. The school will include solar panels, high-performance insulation and natural materials with a low carbon footprint. It is designed as a Nearly Zero Energy Building (NZEB) and aims to use at least 20% less energy than NZEB standards. The building will have flexible learning spaces, green areas, and community facilities.What is being planned for the new primary school in Castel MadamaThe new primary school will replace the existing school on Via della Libertà, ‘O. VULPIANI’, in Castel Madama. The building follows New European Bauhaus principles of beauty, sustainability, and inclusion. Its design includes bright, flexible learning spaces for students and teachers, along with green areas and playgrounds.The building will also be safe and anti-seismic. Public areas will remain available outside school hours, allowing the site to serve purposes beyond regular lessons. The school is currently under construction and is expected to open in the 2026/27 school year. The project is intended to create a modern learning environment while also providing spaces that can be used by the wider community.Around 70% of demolition waste will be reused or recycledThe project takes a circular approach to the materials from the existing school. About 70% of demolition waste from the structure will be reused, recycled, or recovered. This will reduce the amount of material that needs to be discarded during construction.The project will also limit the amount of additional land used for the new building. Its footprint will expand by only 5% compared with the previous one. The approach is designed to retain green areas around the school while making use of the existing site.Along with the treatment of demolition waste, the project includes natural materials with a low carbon footprint. These choices form part of the wider design approach for the new school.How will the new school save energy and resourcesEnergy efficiency is another key part of the new school’s design. The building is planned as a Nearly Zero Energy Building, or NZEB, and aims to consume at least 20% less energy than NZEB standards.High-performance insulation will help support this target, while solar panels will provide renewable energy. The design also includes natural materials with a low carbon footprint. A rainwater and groundwater collection system will form part of the building’s resource management.Together, these features are intended to reduce the school’s energy and resource use. The project also includes a ‘green classroom’ for outdoor learning and environmental education, connecting the school’s design with its surrounding green spaces.Inclusion across learning and communityThe new building is designed to remain useful to the local community beyond school hours. Its public areas, green spaces and playgrounds will be available for cultural, educational and social activities. The design also focuses on accessibility, with ramps, elevators and clear signage to remove architectural barriers.Classrooms and common areas follow the design for all principles, while flexible and modular furniture can adapt to different needs. Students, parents and teachers have taken part in the design process. The Children’s Council also contributed to decisions about classroom layouts, green spaces, learning environments and furniture.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Extreme heat has caused drop in UK milk supply, new data shows
articles.summary: Milk yield was affected by a series of extreme heatwaves which led to poor grazing conditions, researchers say.
articles.body:
Extreme heat this summer has led to dairy farmers delivering 240 million fewer litres of milk than expected, researchers have said.

Farmers delivered four fewer days of milk supply than would be expected between May and August, according to the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit (ECIU).

With the heat leading to poor grazing conditions, stunted harvests and heat strain on livestock in England and Wales, many farmers have started giving winter feed to cattle, including Debbie Wilkins, a dairy and beef farmer in Gloucestershire.

"The costs pile up when you have to bring the cows indoors and the loss of milk production compounds the issue," she said.

Wilkins, who farms in Prior's Norton, said it had been a "difficult" summer.

In total, the ECIU said dairy farmers lost milk valued at more than £83m - enough milk to fill more than one billion school milk cartons.

It follows the UK's hottest summer on record in 2026, with five intense heatwaves and drought declarations.

But while farmers delivered significantly less than expected over the summer, the ECIU said UK milk production could still hit near record levels in 2026.

It said this was because farmers built up a cushion earlier in 2026 which had partially offset the litres lost over the summer.

ECIU said the consolidation of dairy farms in recent years had allowed for "economies of scale and mechanisation to increase milk outputs while the herd size reduces".

Tom Cantillon, a senior analyst at ECIU, said future heatwaves would become progressively harder to recover from, especially as milk was an "unforgiving product in farming" as it cannot be stockpiled.

"The costs don't stop now that the rain has come," Cantillon said.

"A second bad year for grass has pushed farmers into their winter forage early, with feed prices to follow."

Cantillon said farmers needed help to roll out climate resilience measures such as more shade, trees and water.

articles.title: A silver US Army ring missing since 2006 was found in another soldier’s footlocker; after a three-year search, a Fort Worth woman finally returned it to its original owner 20 years later
articles.summary: A silver US army ring that had been missing for two decades is back with the soldier who once wore it, completing a promise a Fort Worth woman made about
articles.body: A silver US army ring that had been missing for two decades is back with the soldier who once wore it, completing a promise a Fort Worth woman made about three years ago. In 2023, when Mary Thelen found the ring, she told NBC 5 Responds that she would keep looking for its owner.A mystery ringShe had found the possession tucked inside an old footlocker belonging to her son, Douglas, who served four tours in Iraq. Douglas did not remember exactly where he found it, thinking it might have been overseas, either in a truck or somewhere in the sand near Baghdad.Finding the owner was made a tad bit easy with the clues on the ring itself. Texas, four aces, the nickname 'T-Bone' and most importantly a name engraved on it: Terry Sheppard Jr. When the outlet shared Thelen's story first in February 2023, it attracted plenty of attention. Online sleuths began contacting a man by that name.“I had a lot of people messaging me on Facebook, just randomly,” Sheppard recalled. “One of my coworkers told me about a story they’d seen, and they were like, ‘You think that’s yours?’” For a while, it seemed the mystery had been solved, but Sheppard and Thelen never connected and the ring remained in her care.But Thelen did not calm down in her efforts and kept searching for the ring's rightful owner. “I can see that this ring belongs to a person who really wants it back, and I really want to meet him,” she said.Back to the ownerThen, during the summer of 2026, Sheppard reached out to NBC 5 seeking help recovering his ring. A few weeks later he and Thelen met each other. “See if you remember that,” Thelen said as she handed him the ring. “Oh, my goodness,” Sheppard replied. “I haven’t seen this in forever.”Sheppard shared that he had not seen the ring since 2006. He ordered it after completing basic training. The design was a personal snapshot of the young soldier he was at the time, featuring his name, his Texas roots and his nickname, 'T-Bone'. “I’m glad it’s back where it belongs,” Thelen told him.While the owner was revealed, what still remained a mystery was how the ring reached somewhere in Iraq. Sheppard never deployed to Iraq, meaning Douglas could not have found the ring there. Moreover, Sheppard added that he had only worn it once or twice. “The last place I can remember having my ring would be Fort Bragg, North Carolina, 82nd Airborne Unit,” he said.It turns out Douglas was also stationed at Fort Bragg during that period. Both men worked in the same area. Sheppard believes he may have removed the ring while working. Douglas likely found it and forgot about it, until his mother uncovered it many years later.Whether Terry and Douglas ever crossed paths remains unknown. “I just never thought I’d actually see this again,” Sheppard said.You use AI every day.
